content: Clubfoot, also referred to as talipes equinovarus (TEV), is a prevalent congenital deformity of the foot. It occurs in approximately 0.64 to 6.8 per 1000 live births, with a male-to-female ratio of 2.5:1. This condition is one of the most common orthopedic abnormalities requiring immediate and comprehensive treatment. Clubfoot causes the foot to turn inward and point downward. While the exact etiology remains unknown, both genetic and environmental factors are believed to contribute to its development. Even after successful treatment, children with TEV often exhibit residual abnormalities, including a shorter and wider foot, a thinner leg, restricted motion of the foot and ankle, reduced strength in the affected limb, gait disturbances, abnormal radiographic findings, and potential limb length discrepancies. Despite these limitations, the primary objective of treatment is to achieve a flexible, plantigrade, pain-free foot that can fit into standard footwear and function effectively. Historically, surgical intervention was the standard approach for managing clubfoot. The most common surgical procedure involved soft tissue release to address the deforming forces within the foot. However, this approach is associated with a high complication rate, which can be challenging to manage. Recurrence of the deformity is the most frequent complication, occurring in approximately 25% of cases (with a range of 13% to 50%). Other complications include infection, neurovascular injury, limb loss, and overcorrection. Non-surgical treatment methods, such as serial casting and manipulation, have since gained prominence. The Kite method was widely used in the past but has been largely replaced by the Ponseti method, which is now the most commonly employed technique worldwide. The Ponseti method typically spans a period of two to four years. It begins with gentle manipulation of the foot, followed by casting to achieve maximum correction. The casts are changed weekly, with a total of five casts applied to correct the adductus and varus deformities by twisting the forefoot inward relative to the heel. In nearly all cases, a percutaneous Achilles tendon tenotomy is performed under local anesthesia to complete the correction. Following this procedure, the foot is immobilized in a cast for three weeks. To maintain the correction, a foot abduction brace is used during nighttime until the child reaches approximately two to four years of age. The ultimate goal of the Ponseti method is to address all components of the deformity, resulting in a pain-free, plantigrade foot with good mobility, free of calluses, and without the need for specialized footwear. This method has been shown to significantly reduce the need for extensive corrective surgery. With appropriate training, healthcare professionals other than surgeons can effectively implement the Ponseti method, making it particularly valuable in regions with limited access to surgical care. The Uganda Sustainable Clubfoot Care Project (USCCP) exemplifies the successful implementation of the Ponseti method in resource-limited settings. This initiative has trained 798 healthcare professionals to identify and treat foot deformities at birth, and Ponseti Clubfoot Care is now available in 21 hospitals across Uganda. Studies have demonstrated that the Ponseti method is equally effective when administered by physiotherapists as when performed by surgeons. Timely treatment of clubfoot in children is crucial. If left untreated, the foot remains twisted inward, leading to pain and functional impairment. Affected children bear weight on the thin skin on the dorsum of the foot, resulting in further deformity and disability. Understanding the effectiveness of the Ponseti method and its functional outcomes compared to traditional surgical approaches is essential for optimizing care for children born with idiopathic congenital clubfoot.
